Consider Frank Ramsey’s proof that there are exactly two Londoners who have exactly the same number of hairs on their heads. Ramsey notes that there are fewer than a million hairs on any one’s head and there are more than a million Londoners. In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), the **pigeonhole principle** states that if n items are put into m containers, with _n_ > _m_, then at least one container must contain more than one item.

[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeonhole_principle#cite_note-3)

In a more quantified version: for [natural numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_number) k and m, if _n_ = _km_ + 1 objects are distributed among m sets, the pigeonhole principle asserts that at least one of the sets will contain at least _k_ + 1 objects.

Advanced mathematical proofs like [Siegel's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel's_lemma) build upon this more general concept.

Pigeons in holes. Here there are _n_ = 10 pigeons in _m_ = 9 holes. Since 10 is greater than 9, the pigeonhole principle says that at least one hole has more than one pigeon. (The top left hole has 2 pigeons.)

In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics"), the **pigeonhole principle** states that if n items are put into m containers, with _n_>_m_, then at least one container must contain more than one item.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeonhole_principle#cite_note-Herstein64-1) For example, of three gloves, at least two must be right-handed or at least two must be left-handed, because there are three objects but only two categories of handedness to put them into. This seemingly obvious statement, a type of [counting argument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics "Combinatorics"), can be used to demonstrate possibly unexpected results. For example, given that the [population of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_London "Demographics of London") is more than one unit greater than the maximum number of hairs that can be on a human head, the principle requires that there must be at least two people in London who have the same number of hairs on their heads.

Although the pigeonhole principle appears as early as 1622 in a book by [Jean Leurechon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Leurechon "Jean Leurechon"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeonhole_principle#cite_note-leurechon-2) it is commonly called **Dirichlet's box principle** or **Dirichlet's drawer principle** after an 1834 treatment of the principle by [Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gustav_Lejeune_Dirichlet "Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet") under the name _Schubfachprinzi

octen.title: Maximal order types for sequences with gap condition
octen.snippet: Higman's lemma states that for any well partial order $X$, the partial order $X^*$ of finite sequences with members from $X$ is also well. By combining results due to Girard as well as Sch\"{u}tte and Simpson, one can show that Higman's lemma is equivalent to arithmetical comprehension over $\textsf{RCA}_0$, the usual base system of reverse mathematics. By incorporating Friedman's gap condition, Sch\"{u}tte and Simpson defined a slightly different order on finite number sequences with fewer comparisons. While it is still true that their definition yields a well partial order, it turns out that arithmetical comprehension is not enough to prove this fact. Gordeev considered a symmetric variation of this gap condition for sequences with members from arbitrary well orders. He could show, over $\textsf{RCA}_0$, that his partial order on sequences is well (for any underlying well order) if and only if arithmetical transfinite recursion is available. We present a new and simpler proof of this fact and extend Gordeev's results to weak and strong gap conditions as well as binary trees with weakly ascending labels. Moreover, we compute the maximal order types of all considered structures. math.LO P. Uftring

## Abstract

We consider the concept of rank as a measure of the vertical levels and positions of elements of partially ordered sets (posets). We are motivated by the need for algorithmic measures on large, real-world hierarchically-structured data objects like the semantic hierarchies of ontological databases. These rarely satisfy the strong property of gradedness, which is required for traditional rank functions to exist. Representing such semantic hierarchies as finite, bounded posets, we recognize the duality of ordered structures to motivate rank functions with respect to verticality both from the bottom and from the top. Our rank functions are thus interval-valued, and always exist, even for non-graded posets, providing order homomorphisms to an interval order on the interval-valued ranks. The concept of rank width arises naturally, allowing us to identify the poset region with point-valued width as its longest graded portion (which we call the “spindle”). A standard interval rank function is naturally motivated both in terms of its extremality and on pragmatic grounds. Its properties are examined, including the relationship to traditional grading and rank functions, and methods to assess comparisons of standard interval-valued ranks.

seltz.snippet: How many mutually compatible tasks can you schedule? How many must remain forever unrelated? This single question, phrased abstractly, drives the theory of chains and antichains. These structures live inside a partially ordered set. Once a set carries an order relation, two extreme kinds of substructure emerge. Chains are substructures where every pair of elements is comparable. Antichains are substructures where no pair is comparable. These are the order-theoretic analogues of "totally sorted lists" and "mutually incomparable items." Together they measure the shape of a poset, the way length and width measure a rectangle. The idea matters because comparability is rarely all-or-nothing. Tasks with dependencies, divisibility among integers, subsets under inclusion, and words under the prefix relation all produce posets. These posets are neither totally ordered nor totally disordered. Chains capture the longest thread of forced sequencing. Antichains capture the largest cluster of tasks that could happen in parallel, with no order constraint among them. The two invariants built from these ideas — height and width — are the first quantitative fingerprints of a poset's structure. The big picture is that height and width are dual lenses on the same object. A chain is a witness that the poset has "depth" in at least one direction. An antichain is a witness that the poset has "breadth" — many elements no rule forces into an order. Later results (most famously Dilworth's Theorem) show that these two notions are tied together by an exact numerical identity. This turns a qualitative distinction into a precise combinatorial law. This article gives the formal definitions of chains, antichains, height, and width. It builds visual intuition via Hasse Diagrams.
